newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Foreign investors upbeat on Bulgarian prospects.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors upbeat on Bulgarian prospects.

text.p: The weekend election victory of the reformist Union of Democratic Forces has boosted economic optimism and Bulgaria might even start thinking about issuing debt on global markets, foreign investors said on Monday.
"There is a changed perception about what is happening in Bulgaria today in financial markets," Salomon Brothers emerging markets research Vice President David Boren told Reuters.
"It is a positive one because of the government's shift in economic policy and active dialogue with the international community," he added.

With all but a handful of results counted, the UDF has won 52 percent of the votes or 137 seats in the 240-seat parliament and is expected to form a government by mid-May which would continue radical reforms launched by the interim cabinet.

"Now we have reform-minded government and not a reform-resistant government and that is crucial for foreign investment," economics director at Credit Suisse First Boston Jonathan Hoffman told Reuters Financial Television.

The new government faces the serious challenge of introducing a self-regulating restrictive monetary mechanism known as a currency board, intended to curb inflation and stabilise the volatile national currency, the lev.

Under a $657 million reform and funding deal sealed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and an interim cabinet, Bulgaria pledged to introduce the currency board in June, speed up privatisation and liberalise prices and trade rules.
"If they can achieve this tremendous task, Bulgarian debt should be the most spectacular performer for the remainder of this year," said Hoffman.
Bulgaria's Brady bonds, issued to restructure an $8.16 billion foreign debt in 1994, were bullish on Monday after news of the UDF victory.
"The caretaker cabinet has given a tremendous platform to the next government," said Hoffman.

The interim cabinet, which took power in February after a government of ex-communist Socialists was forced to step down by mass unrest, brought down monthly inflation to 12 percent in March from 243 percent in February and stopped the free fall of the lev from an all-time low of 3,000 per dollar to around 1,565 now.
Bulgarian officials have said recently they have received offers from major international investment banks to lead manage Bulgarian debt issues on global markets.

"If the situation with the currency board holds and in a few months of its introduction it is functioning properly and the economy is reasonably healthy, it is conceivable to start planning a debt issue in the Eurobond market," said an investment banker who declined to be named.
"More likely it would take place in 1998, but Bulgaria would have to start planning by the middle of this year," the banker added.
Bulgaria would also need to seek improvement of its current Ba3 sovereign debt rating, given by Moody's last October, when the country was on the brink of default, said the banker.

If Bulgaria's credit perception improves as a result of its shift in economic policy, the government could issue debt in a different market from the market it trades in currently to refinance the country's existing debt, economists say. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
